big: Meena reads 'YTM 8%' on a factsheet and plans on ₹80,000 a year from ₹10 lakh. The figure is real. But it is not a promise, and it is not what lands in her account.

lines: The fund's YTM is 8%. So I will get 8%?
YTM is what today's portfolio would earn if every bond were held to maturity and paid as promised. Let us see how a bond's value behaves when you hold it, and when you only look at it each day.

small: 5 years at 8%, if nothing goes wrong
h: Accrual: hold and let it grow
alt: Five bars showing 100 rupees growing at 8% a year for five years
caps: Accrual means buying bonds and holding them to maturity, letting the coupons do the work.
₹100 at an 8% yield grows by about ₹8 in year 1, and a little more each year as it compounds.
This smooth line assumes every payment arrives and the portfolio does not change.
YTM is the best case if all goes as promised. It is not a guarantee.

ylab: ₹100 put in a bond bought at 8%
alt: Two lines of a bond held to maturity: a smooth accrued value and a market price that dips and recovers
caps: One zero-coupon bond bought at 8% and held for ten years. The blue line is its accrued value.
The yellow line is its market price, which moves each day as yields change.
When yields jump above 8%, the market price dips below the accrual line.
A fund must show the yellow line in its NAV. The deepest dip here is about 7%.
Both lines meet at maturity. Held long enough, the accrual wins.

small: 0.6% costs, 31.2% tax, sold after a year
alt: Three bars showing YTM, after expenses and after tax
caps: The factsheet YTM is 8.0%, before anything is taken out.
A 0.6% yearly expense ratio, assumed here, brings it to 7.4%.
Tax at 30% slab with cess, about 31.2% of the gain if sold after a year, leaves 5.1%.
YTM is gross, for today's portfolio. It is not what you keep.

q: Meena puts ₹10 lakh in a fund whose factsheet shows YTM 8%. She expects ₹80,000 after a year. What is the fair way to put it?
opts: It is guaranteed, because YTM is the rate the fund house has promised
Less than ₹80,000 only because of tax, as price moves cancel out
₹80,000 plus all coupons, because YTM covers only the price gain
₹80,000 is a gross estimate, before costs, tax and price moves
why: No rate is promised. YTM assumes every bond is held to maturity and paid in full, and the portfolio itself will change.
Price moves do not cancel out. A rate rise or a downgrade can lower returns, and new buys change the portfolio's yield.
YTM already includes both coupons and the gain or loss to par. Adding coupons on top would count them twice.
YTM describes the current holdings if held to maturity, before expenses and tax. The real result can differ.

q: A fund's portfolio YTM is 8.0%, its expense ratio is 0.6%, and the investor is in the 30% slab, which is 31.2% with cess. If the portfolio earns exactly its YTM and she redeems after a year, about what does she keep?
opts: About 7.4%, which is 8.0% less the 0.6% cost
About 8.0%, because YTM is what the portfolio earns
why: Costs take it to 7.4%. Tax at 31.2% on that gain leaves 5.1%. Real results will vary with prices and the portfolio.
This is after costs but before tax. A slab-rate investor pays tax on the gain, so the figure falls further.
YTM is gross. Costs and tax both come out of it, so an investor never keeps the full factsheet figure.
This skips the 0.6% cost and the 4% cess. Tax of 30% alone on 8.0% would leave 5.6%, but she also pays costs and cess.

q: Meena's short-term accrual fund dips 0.8% in the week after yields rise. She wants to sell, though she planned to hold for about the fund's own duration of two years. What should the adviser explain?
opts: The dip shows that the fund has failed to pay coupons on its bonds
Dips in accrual funds always grow, so selling now is the sound move
A mark-to-market dip; the bonds still pay and mature at face value
NAV cannot fall in an accrual fund, so the statement must be wrong
why: A rate rise explains the dip. A default would be a credit event, and nothing says any coupon has been missed.
Dips do not always grow. Bonds pull back towards face value as maturity nears, so a mark-to-market dip often fades.
Prices are marked daily. The bonds still pay and mature at face value, and her holding period matches the duration.
Accrual funds still mark bonds to market each day, so the NAV can dip when yields rise, even if briefly.

q: A manager lengthens the fund's average maturity from 2 years to 7 because she expects yields to fall. What has changed about how the fund tries to earn?
opts: Nothing, since accrual and duration strategies are the same
It now makes a rate call too, so a rate rise would hurt more
It is now safer, because longer bonds pay more coupons
It now earns a fixed return, since longer bonds lock in the YTM
why: They are different. Accrual earns the coupons, while a duration strategy bets on the path of rates.
A long position pays off if yields fall and hurts if they rise. She is now making a rate call as well as earning coupons.
Longer bonds do pay more yield, but they carry more rate risk. More coupons do not make a fund safer.
Nothing locks in the YTM for a fund. It buys and sells, and longer bonds swing more when yields change.

pts: YTM is not a promised return. It is gross, for today's portfolio, if held to maturity with no default.
Accrual earns the coupons. A duration strategy is a view on rates, and a bad view shows in NAV.
Costs and tax come out of YTM, and a high YTM may signal higher risk.
